text: Every piece of this project has been built and run individually so far — the staging model, its tests, the mart model. dbt build runs all of it together, in one pass, in dependency order. This is the command a real analytics engineer reaches for once a project gets to this point.

Run dbt build. The first line tells you what it found: 2 models, 3 data tests, 1 source — the two real models from Lessons six and eight, the not_null and unique tests from Lesson seven, and the one source from Lesson five.

Here's the real run, line by line. One of four, OK created, the staging model. Two of four, PASS, not_null on customer_id. Three of four, PASS, unique on customer_id. Four of four, OK created, the customers mart. And the line to check first, always: Done, PASS equals 4, WARN 0, ERROR 0, SKIP 0, TOTAL 4. Notice the order — staging first, then its two tests, then the mart last. That's the dependency graph deciding order, not file order.

Here's what would happen if the unique test had failed instead. That line would read FAIL 1, not PASS. And critically, the customers mart model would be SKIPped — not built on top of data already known to be broken. That's the dependency graph protecting the final deliverable: dbt would rather hand back no mart table than one built on a duplicate customer ID.

Here's why this command is the real finish line. Lesson one asked for one thing: a customer list someone could trust. This PASS equals 4, ERROR equals 0 line is the literal, checkable proof that the project met that ask — not a claim, a passing automated check anyone at Jaffle Shop could rerun themselves, any time.

With a clean dbt build behind you, the technical work of this capstone is done. Last lesson, we recap exactly what got built, trace it back to the original ask one more time, and look ahead to the Intermediate capstone, where order history joins this customer table for the first time.
